title: The Good, Bad and Ugly From Buccaneers' 27-24 Loss to Bears
full_text:
Following two consecutive victories for the first time in over a year, the Tampa Bay Buccaneers finally had a little bit of momentum heading into their second primetime game of the 2026 NFL season.
It didn't take long for the Chicago Bears' to squander that momentum, though, as the Bears jumped out to an early 14-0 lead in front of their raucous home crowd at Soldier Field. Despite their offensive struggles in the first half, the Bucs managed to grind their way back into the game thanks to a barrage of splash plays from the defense.
Although the Buccaneers did manage to tie the game with less than three minutes remaining, that was simply too much time to give Ben Johnson's offense, and the Bears won the game by a final score of 27-24.
Let's take a closer look at the good, the bad and the ugly that we saw in this Week 9 matchup between the Buccaneers and Bears .
The rate at which the Buccaneers are turning over their opponents is getting outlandish.
Todd Bowles' defense has generated 13 turnovers over their last three games (yes, you read that correctly). And although producing turnovers at this rate is certainly not sustainable, it sure is fun to watch.
Four of the five Bucs' turnovers on Sunday came via interception, with Tykee Smith providing the first, Zyon McCollum the next two and Alex Anzalone the fourth. The fifth and final turnover came when Rueben Bain Jr. rocked Luther Burden and forced a fumble, which the Bucs recovered deep in Chicago territory.
A defense predicated on consistent pressure and splash plays is how Bowles has always envisioned his defense performing in his dreams, but unfortunately, his worst nightmare appears every time his offense takes the field.
Bucky Irving remains the Buccaneers' most threatening offensive player. Despite a loaded box for much of the game and an entire defensive game plan designed around stopping him, Irving was elusive, relentless and highly productive against a really strong Bears defense.
Irving rushed for 97 yards and two touchdowns to go along with an additional 28 yards through the air on 4 receptions. Even with a non-existent pass game to take the pressure off, Irving refuses to be denied as a ball carrier, and he continues to establish himself as one of the NFL's best all-around running backs.
Mayfield certainly struggled in this football game, but the thumb injury that forced him to miss three games just last month did not appear to limit his ability to throw the football on Sunday.
Baker Mayfield drops it right in the bucket to Tez Johnson 🎯 TBvsCHI on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/XUsnnc2R4S
As encouraging as it was to see Mayfield put some zip on his passes again, his mental processing cost him dearly in this contest.
Mayfield appeared indecisive at times throughout the game and threw two costly interceptions. Unfortunately, this has been the story for Mayfield all season long. And though his injuries have certainly played a role in his poor performance, the vast majority of the issues stem from what's going on between his ears.
Having recently suffered a fractured rib in Week 4 vs. the Packers, which sidelined him for three games, the Bucs were excited to have their star safety, Antoine Winfield Jr., back in the lineup. Unfortunately, Winfield was forced to leave the game on Sunday night after suffering a right ankle injury.
Despite an incredible all-around performance by Bowles' defense, it was a brutal coverage bust on second and long with less than a minute left in the game that allowed Wilson to hit Colston Loveland for a 38-yard gain, ultimately sealing the Bucs' fate.
They forgot about Colston Loveland. pic.twitter.com/mv1rhCXI9a
This headline does not refer to the game of the Buccaneers vs. the Bears, but rather the Buccaneers' offense vs. the Buccaneers' defense.
While Tampa Bay's defense continues to play out of it's mind, the offense simply can't get out of it's own way. It's an incredible contrast between one unit that looks like one of the league's best and the other, which looks like it would have trouble putting up points in the CFL.
What a vicious cycle this game has been. The Bucs’ defense continues to inject life back into this football team while the offense continues to hang them out to dry. Around and around we go.
Although this disheartening dichotomy has plagued the Bucs for most of the season, it was especially evident during Sunday's loss to the Bears, where despite getting five turnovers from the defense, the Buccaneers' offense was only able to generate 10 total points off of those turnovers.

title: Winners and Losers From Buccaneers' Sunday Night Football Loss to Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers defense tried its hardest, but the Bucs offense could not lead the team to a victory on Sunday Night Football.
The Bucs lost their game against the Chicago Bears 27-24 on Sunday, dropping to 3-6. The Bucs' defense managed five turnovers, but the offense got just 10 total points off those turnovers and failed to capitalize on the defense's great game.
Here are our winners and losers for Tampa Bay after this crucial matchup...
It was almost another 100-yard performance for Bucky Irving, but he's a winner tonight for another reason.
Irving ran in a touchdown on Tampa Bay's opening drive of the second half. It was his sixth rushing touchdown of the year, but it was also a touchdown in his hometown of Chicago — this was Irving's first time playing back home, and he gave his family something to remember.
He'll probably never forget scoring a touchdown at Soldier Field, just as he probably dreamed of his whole life growing up. And then after that? He scored again to tie the game with just under three minutes left, cementing this performance as a great one for him.
McCollum had a tough start to his game on Sunday night, getting picked on by Rome Odunze. That didn't last long.
McCollum netted two picks on Caleb Williams across the course of the day. Those turnovers didn't amount to anything (just three points), but that wasn't his fault — he recovered and got the turnovers he need to generate to keep the Bucs in the game.
McCollum has been having an All-Pro year this year, and he kept up the good work on Sunday night. It wasn't enough to win, but that's largely because of the offense and how they handled the game after his turnovers.
Smith was just about everywhere on Sunday night.
He had six total tackles and three solo tackles, and he also had the first interception on the night that kicked off the party. He was one of Tampa Bay's best defensive players, and he really stepped up in the absence of Antoine Winfield Jr. after Winfield went out with an ankle injury.
The Bucs' entire defense balled out, but Smith and McCollum really shined in comparison to the rest.
Bowles' decision-making was costly in this matchup, and it could have cost him the game.
The first questionable decision came on a fourth-and-four at Chicago's four with 14:07 to go in the second. Bowles elected to kick a field goal, but ESPN's analytics model gave the team an extra two percent chance of winning had they gone for it instead of settling for three.
Then, at the end of the half, Bowles elected to kick a field goal instead of trying to score from inside the five with three seconds left. That put Tampa Bay down 17-6 at the half, and the Bucs really could have used those extra points in a tight, tight game against the Bears.
Bowles' defense largely did its job by generating turnovers. But Bowles had to be better with game management, and he wasn't good enough on Sunday.
The last two weeks were easy-going for offensive coordinator Zac Robinson. That wasn't the case on Sunday night, and the offense suffered for it.
Robinson seemed far too comfortable running the ball as a matter of routine as opposed to effectiveness. He put the offense in bad positions early on in the game, and when he had to help facilitate the passing game, he wasn't able to scheme it well enough to help quarterback Baker Mayfield push the ball downfield.
Additionally, the Bucs' offensive line suffered from multiple false starts — that's a problem that the team has been battling all year, and a big part of that is on Robinson, too.
Suddenly, when the Bucs need to throw, Robinson's offense is back to struggling. That's an issue the Bucs are really going to have to face.
It was Baker Mayfield's first game since returning from injury where he really had to throw the football, and it didn't go the way he'd hoped.
Mayfield threw two picks on the night, with one of them going back the other way for a Bears score. The Bucs had four turnovers and, partially due to his efforts, only scored three points off of them.
Mayfield didn't take care of the football, and it was costly. Mayfield has yet to have a great game this year, and that's hurting the offense just as much as Robinson's playcalling has.

title: Buccaneers Could Make Big Step Toward Playoffs With Win vs. Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers and the Chicago Bears are set to face off against each other on Sunday Night Football. It'll be a tough matchup for the Bucs, as the Bears are 6-2 and considered to be Super Bowl contenders at this stage of the season.
The Bucs have an excellent defense, however — the best in the league by numerous advanced metrics — and they've developed a running game that has punished teams in the NFC South, the Carolina Panthers and the Atlanta Falcons, in recent weeks.
It's going to be hard to beat the Bears. But after the New Orleans Saints beat the Cleveland Browns in overtime on Sunday afternoon, the NFC South is in a unique scenario, and the Bucs can take advantage.
The Buccaneers are currently involved in a complete four-way tie for first in the NFC South. Every team in the division has three wins, and the Bucs have yet to play until Sunday night.
At the moment, the Bucs lead the division. They've played one more game than the Panthers, but because the Bucs play late, they've played the same number of games until 8:20 p.m. tonight. The Bucs have the tiebreaker win over the Panthers and have also beaten the Falcons for two NFC South wins, so they're up in front in the four-way tiebreaker.
The good news for the Bucs? If they beat the Bears on Sunday night, they'll move to 4-5 — that would be the best record in the NFC South by itself, and the Bucs would move into sole possession of first place.
If the Bucs don't win, though, the news isn't all too bad. Tampa Bay will be 3-6, and every NFC South team will have the same number of wins. The Panthers and Saints will have one less loss, though, because both have had their bye week already, so the Bucs would remain half a game out of the NFC South lead behind the Panthers.
Tampa Bay has its bye week next week. As a result, the Falcons, Saints and Panthers could take possession of first place while the Bucs take the week off in Week 10.
Tampa Bay plays the Bears in Soldier Field at 8:20 p.m. on Sunday night. A win would be huge, but if the Bucs drop this game to a Super Bowl contender, they're still in shape to fight for the South.

title: Sunday Night Football Injury Update: Will Emeka Egbuka Play for Buccaneers?
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have one of the biggest challenges of the year ahead of them when they play the Chicago Bears on the road. The Bears are 6-2 and a Super Bowl contender — the Bucs are 3-5 and, despite the record, still very much in the hunt for the NFC South,
The Bucs will want every player they can muster to help beat Chicago. There's one player they won't have for certain, as edge rusher Yaya Diaby sprained his MCL last week against the Atlanta Falcons and was ruled out for this contest.
One other player was ruled questionable, though. Wideout Emeka Egbuka has missed the last two games of the year with a foot injury, and he practiced in full on Thursday and Friday. So will he play for the Bucs on Sunday? Or will their passing offense have to make do without him?
The NFL's Ian Rapoport reported on Sunday that Egbuka is set to play against the Bears on Sunday night.
#Bucs WR Emeka Egbuka (foot) is playing today after being listed as questionable. He missed Wednesday but was a full participant after that.
The move is expected. Egbuka has been recovering from both a concussion and a foot injury these past two weeks — he cleared concussion protocol last week, but his foot injury lingered. Now that he's practiced two days in full, he's definitely set to play against the Bears in a game where the Bucs need him.
Egbuka hasn't been the leading wide receiver the Bucs have perhaps hoped this year, netting 28 receptions for 240 yards and two touchdowns, but the entire passing game has struggled so far for Tampa Bay.
Egbuka will still be a good weapon for Tampa Bay, as they'll need to pass the ball to beat the Bears after throwing just 14 total passes in the last two weeks of play. Quarterback Baker Mayfield should get his first real test at throwing the ball after dislocating his thumb in Week 3 against the Minnesota Vikings.
The Bucs play the Bears in Soldier Field at 8:20 p.m. on Sunday night. When they do, they'll have their first-round pick from 2025 at their disposal.

title: One Major Question Could Define the Bucs' Entire Night Against Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers' defense has stepped it up in recent weeks, particularly along the defensive front. And they will once again need that same presence in Week 9 as they will face one of the premier offenses in the league — the Chicago Bears.
The Bucs' pass rush has ramped it up as of late, exploding for 10 sacks over their past three games after a quiet start to the year. Through eight games, they have 23 sacks this season.
Tampa's resurgence in creating pressure has been a blessing for them, but they will need to continue that when they face the Bears' elite offense led by star quarterback Caleb Williams.
Todd Bowles' defense ranks near the top of the league when it comes to bringing the blitz, sending extra rushers over 40% of the time. The Bucs' front seven will have to create pressure with just four, but bringing an extra guy has proven to work, given how well the secondary has played.
If they are unable to get pressure and get home, it will allow Williams plenty of time to find his open targets in Luther Burden III, Rome Odunze and Colston Loveland. The Bears are a top-three team in the NFL with time to throw (3+ seconds to throw).
Tampa Bay hasn't relied on one star to get home for sacks this year, rather relying on its depth of coordinated packages of Yaya Diaby, Rueben Bain Jr., David Walker, Al-Quadin Muhammad and Anthony Nelson.
Chicago has been vulnerable to sacks on the season when interior gaps collapse, allowing 19 on the season. If the Bucs' interior defensive line of Vita Vea and Calijah Kancey can continue getting push up the middle, it will force Williams off his spot, ultimately disrupting his timing within passing concepts.
With the Bucs' offense being run-dependent, the defense has carried the load of keeping the game close and low-scoring. If the pass rush isn't able to stop the high-flying offense of Chicago, it will force Baker Mayfield to throw the ball.
If Tampa Bay hopes to keep the game close and come away with a statement victory, the pass rush must get home to keep Williams out of his comfort zone.

title: Our Buccaneers vs. Bears Score Predictions Are In
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have one of their hardest games on the schedule coming up this weekend, playing the Chicago Bears on Sunday Night Football in prime time on the road. The Bucs are 3-5, and a win over this Bears team would give them a big boost before their bye.
It certainly won't be easy, though, and our staff doesn't think so, either. As always, our picks are in for this upcoming matchup — here's how we see this crucial Week 9 game turning out:
The Bucs have ripped off two straight W’s and know their identity is built on the run game and great defense. They will need both vs. the Bears on SNF.
Chicago owns one of the best offenses in the league, led by Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams, and their defense got even more stout up front with the addition of Jeffrey Simmons.
However, the Bucs can exploit their secondary, which means Baker Mayfield will have to throw the ball. It will be the real first test of his thumb.
I think the Bucs are able to keep things close despite this being a tough challenge. However, they fall just short.
This is a game where I think the Bucs fall back down to earth a little bit. The team is facing one of the best offenses in the NFL that just had a great defensive showing against the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks. If Baker Mayfield and the passing game can’t get going, this could be a long game.
For the first time in over a year, the Bucs have won back-to-back games. It's a step in the right direction, sure, but they've still got a lot of work to do to dig themselves out of the hole they created for themselves by going 0-4 to start the season.
We still don't really know if Baker Mayfield can throw the ball down the field after returning from his thumb injury, and the Bears present all sorts of problems on both sides of the ball. The Bucs' defense may be legit, but that won't be enough to knock off the Bears in Chicago.
I’m getting my popcorn out for the battle between Todd Bowles’ defense and Ben Johnson’s offense. This is going to be fun.
I think it’s going to be a close-scoring game, but Baker Mayfield is going to have to shake off the rust, which he told us earlier this week shouldn’t be an issue. Still, it’s gonna have to get going a bit to allow for the run game to open up.
Stopping Caleb Williams won’t be easy, but right now, Bowles has been the old Bowles we all know — terrorizing offenses.
I think Tampa Bay keeps it close but in the end, on prime time, they don’t pull it off.
Every week, I doubt Tampa Bay, and the last two weeks, they've proven me wrong. Were it another opponent, I would be more open to picking Tampa Bay this time around — but this Chicago Bears team is very, very good.
Caleb Williams is unstoppable when he isn't getting in his own way, and he's been crisp and consistent for two weeks. Ben Johnson is the best playcaller in football, and the Bears will be defending home turf after a big win against Seattle the Monday prior.
The Bucs have a strong running game and an elite defense. But the passing game remains nonexistent (literally, in some cases), and the offense won't be enough to outscore the Bears in this contest.
Things were more even last week, but this week, our staff is all Bears. We're betting that Chicago's well-rounded team and the addition of Jeffery Simmons will be enough to knock off a Bucs team still looking to find its identity.
That being said, the Bucs have a chance with this defense. And if they win? Tampa Bay's momentum couldn't be higher entering the bye week.

title: Bucs Fans May Not Want to Hear This Before Game Against Bears
full_text:
The Tampa Bay Buccaneers will get one heck of a challenge when they head to Chicago to take on the Bears on Sunday Night Football.
The Bucs are riding in hot after back-to-back division wins and will come into this primetime matchup relying heavily on their running game and defensive prowess.
The Bears, in their own right, look to be one of the true Super Bowl contenders in the league and will provide the Bucs with their toughest challenge over the past few weeks.
The Bucs have beaten the struggling Carolina Panthers and an Atlanta Falcons team that imploded, but they have yet to get the test of a disciplined, high-functioning contender like the Bears over the past few weeks.
Unlike the Panthers and Falcons, the Bears offense isn't really one-dimensional or focused on one player. Carolina and Atlanta's offenses couldn't really push the ball down the field against Todd Bowles' defense, but Chicago's multifaceted playmakers can attack both horizontally and vertically, making it tough for defenses to cover the entire field.
While the Bears' offense has been their strong suit, they also boast one of the better run-stopping defenses in the league thanks to their strong defensive front.
The Bucs' offensive line was able to bully the Panthers' and Falcons' defensive fronts with gap schemes and heavy run scripts. However, the Bears' front seven have surrendered under 88 yards per game to opponents.
With heavy-hitters like Montez Sweat and recently acquired Jeffery Simmons anchoring the defensive line, Tampa Bay won't be able to just line up and lean on Bucky Irving and Kenny Gainwell as they did against softer defensive fronts.
The Buccaneers have made history over the past few weeks by not putting the ball in the air with Baker Mayfield, but they will likely have to do so against Chicago.
While the Bears' defensive front is their strength, they are susceptible in their secondary and Zac Robinson must know how to creatively mix in the pass to create balance on the offensive side of the ball.
Shifting from non-primetime games over the past couple of weeks to the brightest lights on Sunday, it will be a true litmus test for where the Bucs are. While it will be a struggle, this could be a typical NFL spot where the Bears don't take Tampa seriously.
The Bucs are far from a finished product, but coming away with a victory over one of the elites in the NFL would do wonders for the psyche of the team and the confidence that they can make some noise the rest of the way.

full_text:
We're now just a little over four hours out from the NFL trade deadline. At this point, we've exhausted our predictive brains and are waiting on the Tennessee Titans to either make a move or stand pat when the 3:00 PM CT cutoff strikes.
As of this morning, our latest update came in the form of a confirmation from Jordan Schultz: Tennessee is not looking to move RB Tony Pollard. He's become almost too crucial to Cam Ward and the offense to be sent packing at the midway point this season.
However, it's worth noting that Albert Breer said it would take "at least a fourth-rounder, and maybe a third" to get Pollard out of Nashville. Breer also admitted that Tennessee "won't give him away," but a different source setting a price there is notable.
If the Colts ultimately refuse to trade Jonathan Taylor, Pollard's value could skyrocket at the buzzer. Past Pollard, the Titans' outlook is mostly up in the air. That trio set aside, DE Jermaine Johnson is a name fans should keep an eye on. There has been minimal noise surrounding Johnson, but he's in the final year of his contract and could be argued as an asset worth moving for the Titans to stack more draft capital. LB Cody Barton should be tabbed for similar reasons.
It's straw-grasping from there. We'll keep you looped in as news comes in today, Titans fans. Check back here for the latest.

title: 1 Final Prediction: Forecasting the Landing Spot, and Haul, for Titans' Leading Trade Candidate
full_text:
It's become increasingly obvious that if the Tennessee Titans are going to try to move anyone today, it's pass-catcher Calvin Ridley. Sure, we could see a surprise offer come in for one of Tennessee's numerous pieces of defensive depth, or a team could get desperate and throw something crazy out there for RB Tony Pollard.
But as of right now, Ridley is the only name that keeps coming up as one that the Titans would be open and willing to part with. Now tha t the trade deadline is just a few hours away, news regarding this potential move could pop at any time.
Past the likelihoods and the expectations, though, is a deal that actually has to get done. We circled three suitors as primary candidates to trade for Ridley earlier this week; the Kansas City Chiefs, the Pittsburgh Steelers, and the San Francisco 49ers.
Now that another round of football has been played, I'm making the argument that one of those teams has pulled away. In today's last-second prediction, I have the Kansas City Chiefs sending Tennessee a sixth-round pick to secure Ridley prior to the deadline.
The stars are aligning for this move, and it makes sense for either side.
Rising receiver Xavier Worthy left Kasnas City's Week 9 victory over the New York Jets with a hamstring injury, exasperating the team's need at WR to an even further degree. The Chiefs had just returned leading pass-catcher Rashee Rice after he missed multiple weeks earlier this year.
WR Tyquan Thornton is on IR due to a severe ankle injury he sustained earlier this season; backup options Jeff Caldwell and Jimmy Holiday are also off the board. That leaves Kansas City with little choice but to add to that dwindling room.
Ridley may not have a place in Brian Daboll's offense any longer, but a move west could offer the 31-year old new life. Where the Titans are drafting and signing younger talent for their WR core as a part of an overarching rebuild, the Chiefs are grasping at a (mostly) bygone era of success to try and win another championship.
Their franchise makeup is opposite to Tennessee's. Where the Titans are tearing old pillars down, the Chiefs are gluing and taping them together to try and squeeze another title run or two out of the rubble.
Thus far, it's worked. Kansas City is 6-2. But with the Chiefs openly looking to get stronger at WR, per Zachary Pereles, it's clear they're currently short of the intended mark. The sixth-round asking price for Ridley emerged earlier this week as a sign that Tennessee is ready to move on from him.
Kansas City can certainly afford that tag, and if they strike out on someone like Brian Thomas Jr., taking a flyer on Ridley could be their easiest remaining choice. I think it's more likely than not that we see Ridley moved today, and I'm projecting Kansas City as his eventual destination.

title: Addition by Subtraction: How Titans’ LB Room is 1 Trade Away From an Upgrade
full_text:
The Tennessee Titans enjoyed a bye in Week 9, but will get back to work in Week 10 against the Jacksonville Jaguars. However, before Sunday's home contest, Tennessee will need to make decisions on the futures of multiple veteran players.
With the Titans sitting at 1-7 and the trade deadline set for Tuesday at 4 p.m. ET, general manager Mike Borgonzi has gotten plenty of calls on the team's veteran pieces who could provide value to contending squads. The common names mentioned in trade discussions have been running back Tony Pollard, safety Amani Hooker, and wide receiver Calvin Ridley.
One player who hasn't been brought up in trade rumors is linebacker Cody Barton, which is surprising. Barton should be one of Tennessee's top trade candidates ahead of the deadline, as moving on from the veteran linebacker makes a ton of sense.
Barton has been a serviceable starter for the Titans this season, tallying 34 tackles and 16 defensive stops with a 62.4 Pro Football Focus grade . As a result, the former Denver Bronco could net Tennessee a solid return on the market, and trading him makes sense given the state of the linebacker room.
Cedric Gray set the Titans franchise record in combined tackles in 2025 with 164. However, Gray has been demoted to a limited rotational role this year, as rookie Anthony Hill Jr. is the starter next to Barton. Though he has endured some of the usual rookie growing pains, Hill has shown promise this year as a potential long-term starter on the Titans' defense. The Texas product has already posted 82 tackles and 24 defensive stops in eight games , but has struggled in coverage.
Regardless, Hill is a defensive piece Tennessee can build around, and it would be wise for the Titans to roll into the future with him and Gray as the starters. Barton's experience is a nice plus, but Gray is more talented, better in pass coverage, and should be the starter.
Barton doesn't offer much upside for the future, and it's strange that head coach Robert Saleh and defensive coordinator Gus Bradley are playing the 29-year-old over the high-potential Gray. As a result, Tennessee should be shopping Barton and looking to send him to a linebacker-needy team to clear the way for Gray to reclaim his starting spot.
We'll see whether Barton is still on the Titans roster after 4 p.m. ET Tuesday. Barton isn't a negative on Saleh's defense, but Gray should be seeing more reps next to Hill.
Dharya Sharma is a sportswriter from Nebraska who has been covering the Tennessee Titans through his website, SharmSports, since 2023. He is also an NFL and NBA writer for The Sporting News and had a previous stop with Sportsnaut. Follow him on X @SharmSports

title: Setting a Price for 5 Titans Trade Candidates Before Tomorrow's Deadline
full_text:
With the trade deadline looming near, many fans are wondering just how active the Titans are going to be. Obviously, they won’t be buyers right now, but this team has plenty of pieces that other teams are surely interested in.
The Ringer’s Tom Pelissero noted that we could see up to 10 trades before Tuesday’s deadline. If that does in fact come to fruition, then it's hardly an exaggeration to say we could be in store for one of the most chaotic trade deadlines in recent history.
During Monday’s press conference, Robert Saleh said that barring unforeseen circumstances, the team they have now will be the one they roll into next Sunday with. Meaning, he’s not expecting any trades between now and the deadline. However, until we get there, speculation will undoubtedly continue to run rampant.
Therefore, I'm going to discuss the Titans’ likeliest trade candidates heading into Tuesday , and what it should take for the team to realistically move on from them if that possibility remains on the table.
This is clearly the most polarizing of all the realistic trade candidates. Some fans believe the Titans should trade him while his value appears to be at its highest, while others believe he’s too important for QB Cam Ward’s development to trade.
I fall under the latter in this situation. Right now, Ward’s only consistent weapons through eight games have been rookie WR Carnell Tate and RB Tony Pollard. Taking half of those away could ultimately be setting Ward up for failure for the rest of the season.
Especially with there being no reliable option behind Pollard at the moment. Not having a consistent ground game will make an already struggling offense completely one-dimensional, which in turn will make defenses hone in on the Titans’ pass catchers, subsequently making Ward’s job way harder than it already is.
The only way you can justify making a move like this is if the return is simply too good to pass up. You can justify trading Pollard for a top-100 pick since that will put you in prime position to get his long-term replacement next Spring without having to sacrifice one of the premium picks you already have.
Getting an extra third-round pick would give the Titans five picks over the first three rounds, three of which are on day two of the draft. If that were the case, it would not shock me one bit if the Titans went ahead and spent one of those picks on someone they believe could be the Titans’ next great running back.
What you won’t be able to justify is potentially sabotaging the most important player on the team solely to get an extra day three pick in return.
The only way the Titans can afford to trade Pollard is if they get something truly valuable in return. Otherwise, this isn’t a move worth making at this particular time, and that's being actively reflected by the team's stubborn attitude toward the move.
Hooker is playing the best ball of his career right now, so it’s easy to see why contending teams are interested in his services. He’s currently tied for the most interceptions in the NFL (five), while also earning an overall grade of 81 (sixth highest) through eight games, per PFF.
Hooker also has an impressive grade against the run (83.9), making him one of the most well-rounded safeties in the league, who also happens to be under contract through the 2028 season.
If the Titans are gonna part ways with someone as valuable and talented as Hooker, the return needs to be substantial. I would try to get a conditional third-round pick that could potentially turn into a second rounder, while ultimately settling for an unconditional third-round pick at absolute worst.
If nobody is willing to meet that price, then the Titans will have no problem keeping Hooker around for the foreseeable future.
Martin has been one of the genuine surprises of the season. When he signed with the Titans back in March, I don’t think even the most optimistic fan could’ve predicted how impactful he would be. Martin has recorded 6.5 sacks in eight games, which is tied with Vikings LB Andrew Van Ginkel for the eighth most in the league.
The veteran pass rusher could be an intriguing addition for a contending team looking to bolster their depth along the edge. With Martin under contract for another year, I would try to get an early day three pick in return.
Getting offered a fifth-round pick is probably more likely, but if I’m moving off my most consistent pass rusher who also happens to be top-10 in sacks, then I think it’s more than fair to want at least a fourth-rounder in return.
With Johnson not under contract beyond this season, I think the only way to get a fourth-round pick out of him would be to throw some conditions on the trade, similarly to what they did with OLB Dre’Mont Jones last season.
Last year, the Titans traded Jones for a conditional fifth-round pick that could turn into a fourth-round selection if the Ravens made the playoffs and Jones records at least two sacks in the regular season. The latter of which he accomplished.
I think something similar for Johnson would be fair, although I don’t see this one happening. The Florida State product has recorded three sacks and five tackles for loss, resulting in an overall grade of 64.2 through eight games, per PFF .
Simply put, moving on from Ridley would be mutually beneficial for everybody involved. Ridley could join a team he’s probably better suited for, while the Titans can get an extra draft pick in return to take another shot at finding a diamond in the rough towards the end of day three.
Ridley has less than 100 yards receiving this season, and it’s clear the Titans favor their young receivers at this point, as they should.
If someone offers the Titans a 2027 or even a 2028 7th-round pick, I think the wise move would be to just take it and move on.
Shaun is a longtime Titans fan who has years of experience in the field. He missed being on the team beat, and is here to change that. He also writes scripts for EA Sports' Madden games, where fans may have heard his work.

title: Final Titans NFL Trade Deadline Big Board: 1 Must-Trade and 4 Outside Possibilities
full_text:
The NFL trade deadline is now just one day and a handful of hours away. Robert Saleh said this morning that the Tennessee Titans are operating as if the roster right now will take the field next Sunday, but we all know it's more complicated than that.
Our last trade big board for the Titans saw seven candidates I believed could be in contention. Now much closer to the deadline, I've whittled that list down and seperated the remaining five candidates into two categories.
Those are the must-trade category, as well as outside possibilities. We'll start with the much shorter former one first.
Calvin Ridley is both the only player that looks especially likely to be moved at this point, and the only one that Tennessee should be trying to trade. You can make a positive case for almost anyone else on this list, but Ridley is essentially a non-factor.
The veteran WR has just six catches on the year, although he's only missed one game. Ridley's inability to find his footing in OC Brian Daboll's offense has resulted in multiple costly drops and a steady decline in opportunities.
As of yesterday, the Titans are still listening to offers on Ridley. A sixth-round pick seems to be the going rate, and there are multiple teams that could sensibly fork over the draft capital to bulk up their postseason chances this year.
Tennessee should seek those teams out and get a deal done by tomorrow at almost any cost.
Now to the guys who will probably stick around... but it's worth visiting the prospect of a trade anyway. Tony Pollard is the elephant in the room, and has all been all season.
It's evident by this point that the Titans aren't looking to trade Pollard. He's become Cam Ward's right-hand man in the backfield, and it seems that Tennessee are intent on keeping him there until his contract expires this offseason.
If the backfield market gets desperate enough, I could see a wild offer convincing Tennessee to go ahead and make the move. A third-round pick, or a package deal, would be hard to turn down.
But the key word there is "convincing." As of right now, Pollard remains an outside possibility because the Titans don't want to trade him. Fans should expect the veteran RB to remain in his leading role barring an unexpected haul.
Jermaine Johnson has been posed as a sort of quiet possibility for Tennessee as we get close to the deadline. There has been little noise surrounding a potential trade with Johnson, but the EDGE certainly fits the bill of someone who could be on the chopping block.
He's in the final year of his rookie contract on a roster ready to turn things over for another reset at any time. Johnson's past connections to Robert Saleh, due to their shared time with the New York Jets, make the opposite argument and provide some staying power.
If Jeffery Simmons hadn't been moved, Johnson would most likely have been a more prominent candidate. As things stand, he's an outside shot with a large role in this defense due to Simmons' absence.
Tennessee is between a rock and a hard place here. It's more probable that he stays, but with fellow d-lineman Jacob Martin heavily outpacing Johnson, the 27-year old rusher is worth mentioning as a potential surprise trade.
Per Jeremy Fowler this morning, the Titans have received calls on S Amani Hooker but don't want to move him. After his three-INT performance against the Cincinnati Bengals in Week 8, Hooker leads the NFL in interceptions with five.
Hooker is 28 years old and under contract with Tennessee through 2028. At this point, he's one of the most valuable assets in Saleh's unit and clearly has gas left in the tank. The kicker, of course, is that he'd arguably bring in the heftiest trade return (save for Pollard) of anyone left on this list.
Like Pollard, the Titans aren't looking to make a move here; it would take a strong offer the likes of which Tennessee hasn't yet seen to drum up any momentum around Hooker. I hesitate to call anyone truly "untouchable" on a 1-7 roster, but Hooker appears to be about as close as you can get with the Titans.
This is as wild a shot in the dark as they come, but our own Isaiah Pinto made an argument for the Titans to move on from Tyjae Spears. Despite there being no noise in this direction, the train of thought is definitely there.
Spears has two total touches in the last three weeks of Titans football. The backup RB's knee issues have kept him at bay this season, but even when he's seen the field (six of eight games), Spears hasn't been able to find a remote groove.
Between the Titans drafting rookie back Nick Singleton last year and probably retaining Pollard the rest of the way, Spears looks like an outlier now and in the future. That isn't even taking into account the possibility that the Titans use a first-round pick on a back in next year's draft.
Spears' age (25) and inexpensive contract could make him a sneakily compelling choice for a team in need of backfield help at the deadline. Given the aforementioned factors, Spears may not be too hard to pry from the Titans' grasp, either.
Not a surefire candidate by any means, but an inarguably sensible one on paper.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Making a Bold Trade Suggestion for Titans if Tony Pollard Won't be Moved: Another RB Goes Instead
full_text:
There are numerous names swirling around the NFL's upcoming trade deadline, with the Titans being one of the biggest expected sellers. The cutoff is at 3 PM CT on November 10.
After trading their franchise best player and multi-time All-Pro DT Jeffery Simmons to the Chicago Bears two weeks ago, many pundits are anticipating Tennessee to seek more draft capital with a 1-7 record. Names like WR Calvin Ridley, RB Tony Pollard, and S Amani Hooker are considered to be the Titans' most notable trade candidates, although the only one with real momentum is Ridley.
In fact, as of now, the Titans have no plans to trade Pollard or Hooker in spite of interest in each. However, there's a young and talented running back that has been oddly benched that a team looking for depth should take a flier on. It's Tyjae Spears.
Entering his fourth NFL season, Spears looked to serve as a viable asset in the Tennessee Titans offense. Many anticipated Spears would take over as starter with Pollard in his age 29 season on an expiring contract.
This is still possible, but recently Pollard has been dominating for the Titans, leaving Spears with back-to-back healthy scratches against the Browns and Bengals. In those two games, Pollard went off. He combined for nearly 300 yards from scrimmage and five touchdowns. The vet has earned the complete trust of OC Brian Daboll.
Unfortunately for Spears, he has slowly seen the field less and less over the course of the season. This year on the whole, Pollard has 296 offensive snaps to Spears' 140, according to Fantasy Pros .
It was only a few weeks ago, in Week 5, when Spears recorded a team-high nine receptions against the Houston Texans, serving as QB Cam Ward's reliable backfield target. Since that game, the former third-round pick has only been given two touches total.
Earlier in the season, Spears proved to have versatility as a pass blocker and a receiving back with 15 receptions for 75 yards and zero drops.
Despite not playing the last two weeks, Spears has more receptions than Pollard, WR Elic Ayomanor, WR Chimere Dike, TE Daniel Bellinger and Ridley, for the team's fourth-most catches. As a runner, Spears has a career average of 4.1 yards per carry with eight touchdowns and only two fumbles. Although his stats may not jump off the page, Spears certainly isn't a one-tool running back.
Currently, the two highly sought-after running backs at the deadline are Saquon Barkley and Jonathan Taylor, who both have contracts through 2028 worth more than $35 million, per Spotrac . Furthermore, Barkley turns 30 in February and Taylor turns 28 in January, and most running backs don't play far into their 30s as a general rule of thumb
Barkley and Taylor may have continuous success in future seasons, but they are two of the top four highest-paid players at their position. Giving up draft capital for stars considered to be entering the latter years of their careers is a gamble.
Meanwhile, Spears is on the last year of his rookie contract, worth roughly $1.4 million this season. His age and inexpensive contract makes Spears an attractive under-the-radar trade candidate looking to add depth to their backfield.
If Tennessee's coaching staff isn't going to play Spears, why keep him?
The Titans have shown a strong liking for Pollard, especially in the last three games, and his recent breakout performances may have won over the organization. Consequently, Spears could find himself in a new uniform next week before Tennessee overhauls their backfield next season.
Isaiah is an award-winning journalist and photojournalist. A graduate from the University of Kentucky, he has previously been published by BloodHorse, KY Insider, and the Kentucky Kernel for multimedia sports coverage. Isaiah is a Tennessee Volunteer at heart bringing his local expertise to Titans coverage.

title: 1 Move the Titans Can't Afford to Get Wrong at the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
Two days (a little less now) out from the NFL trade deadline at 3:00 PM CT on November 10, the only real noise-maker remaining for the Tennessee Titans is Calvin Ridley. RB Tony Pollard and S Amani Hooker have basically fallen off the board, leaving the veteran WR as the team's lone likely candidate.
Although, there are a few possibilities that shine through the cracks. A 1-7 squad can't really be held to any standard if the right team comes calling. Take the Jeffery Simmons trade, which nobody saw coming, as the strongest argument to that end.
Now, enter DE Jermaine Johnson. The former New York Jet and Robert Saleh pupil is only in his first year with Tennessee. He was acquired in an offseason trade earlier this year that would set him up to play out the final year of his contract on Nashville.
Naturally, the closer we get to the end of that deal, the bigger the questions are about the Titans' plans with Johnson. He's a tradable player, even if the buzz surrounding that potential move has been limited to completely silent.
But this is a move the Titans would have to approach oh-so carefully.
Trading Tony Pollard would be one thing; the veteran RB is in the final year of his deal, and at 29 years old, really only has utility for the rest of this season. That utility is tied to Cam Ward's growth, though, which makes him a more valuable asset.
Johnson paints a less clear picture. He's only 27 years old, evidenced by him currently being in the fifth year of his rookie deal. His ties to Coach Saleh make his role more interesting, and Johnson's three sacks on the year are good for second on the roster right now.
The DE rides the line between a compelling long-term piece and someone who Tennessee could bear to part with for the right price. Especially because Saleh isn't guaranteed a spot on the sideline forever, someone brought in for his system could appear less compelling if things keep ticking down.
Ridley is a holdover from the Brian Callahan era, and again, he's by far the biggest name on the Titans' trade block. The Titans can't sell Johnson too low, as trading Simmons put even greater pressure on the DE.
But just like anyone else on this roster, if not more so, Johnson shouldn't be a can't-touch player. Perhaps in spite of Saleh's own post-bye aspirations, this is an incomplete Titans team sprinting toward another draft-first reset.
That puts guys like Johnson (and Pollard for that matter) in an awkward spot. It also makes the decision about Johnson at the deadline all the more important.

title: Titans Not Looking to Trade Tony Pollard — But What Would an Undeniable Offer Look Like?
full_text:
With Adam Schefter reporting today (in the middle of some push-ups) that the Tennessee Titans outright won't be trading RB Tony Pollard, noise surrounding the veteran playmaker has died down considerably. A guy who had once been the Titans' primary trade candidate seemed to have played himself into an untouchable spot.
But Jeffery Simmons once appeared to be in that spot also, until the Chicago Bears made an undeniable offer. The Titans were even turning down inquiries from the New York Giants for Simmons, which is another debacle that we'd rather leave untouched.
If Jonathan Taylor ends up being off the table, would it be at all possible for the Titans to see a similarly undeniable offer come through for Pollard? Tennessee wouldn't get two-first round selections in a million years, but that doesn't have to be the standard for a rebuilding roster.
The opposite side of the no-trade argument is that, no matter what happens the rest of this season, Pollard will likely be a big-ticket free agent that Tennessee won't bring back. He's only being held now because his consistency in the backfield gives Cam Ward a reliable playmaking floor on offense.
If Simmons can go at the right price, Pollard can too.
A fourth-rounder alone may not do it, but what about a fourth and a later pick? Could a third-round selection get the job done? If a team is confident that Pollard would resign, and desperately need help in the backfield, an unprecedented second-round selection would almost certainly sway Tennessee into decisive territory.
Now, I can't imagine the latter becomes a reality. However, the RB market particularly is alive and well. Just to name a few teams dealing with injuries at the position: The Arizona Cardinals, the Miami Dolphins, the Houston Texans, the Jacksonville Jaguars, and the New York Giants.
If we're strictly talking undeniable pitches, a second-round pick is the only thing that comes to mind within the remote realm of reason - and it's still a stretch. The Titans would at least have to look twice at anything higher than a fourth, or at a package deal of some sort.
This isn't even considering the possibility that other players could be involved. Schefter's words make a Pollard trade unlikely, without a doubt, but Titans fans shouldn't rule out any move until the deadline buzzer sounds on Tuesday. One-win teams are among the easiest to persuade.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: How Titans' Most Expected Trade Deadline Move Could Lead to Win Over Jaguars in Week 10
full_text:
The trade deadline is now just over 48 hours away, and the Tennessee Titans are one of two teams coming down to the wire on their bye week. Coming off what may have been their best game of the season in a Week 8 loss, Tennessee has a real opportunity to build with time off.
That includes addition by subtraction, in this case. Stacking reports over the past few days have painted the picture that Tennessee is likely to move veteran WR Calvin Ridley. Not only would that trade be positive for the franchise, but it could help boost the Titans to an upset win in Week 10.
I've already taken a dive into just how difficult the home matchup with the Jacksonville Jaguars is shaping up to be out of the bye. The Jags are 6-2 (today's game pending) and have an iron grip on the AFC South. The 1-7 Titans are heavy underdogs on paper.
But Tennessee wasn't expected to take the Cincinnati Bengals to overtime last week, either. Tennessee wasn't expected to score 36 points. I believe Ridley being out of the picture paves the way for a repeat performance from the offense.
Why? Simply put: Better, more fitting receivers will get an extended chance to shine. We got a peek at this outcome in Week 8, when second-year WR and return specialist Chimere Dike nearly matched Ridley's season-long catch total in one showing.
Dike's five receptions for 71 yards and a score shone light on a connection with Cam Ward that we'd hardly seen this year; that strong performance even came without leading receiver Carnell Tate, who should return to the lineup in Week 10.
What happens when the Titans add Tate, retain Dike in a primary role, and subtract Ridley? You've got a younger, more cohesive unit geared toward replicating their breakout showing vs. Cincy.
Of course, much more will have to fall Tennessee's way to topple the top team in their division. I'd like to think the Titans hold on to Tony Pollard at the deadline, and that Brian Daboll will scheme more for TE Gunnar Helm in a further effort to build on last week.
Jacksonville has also scored 30+ points in three straight games, and have won two in a row. To say that Robert Saleh's defense will have their jobs cut out for them for the second game in a row would be wildly understating it.
All the same, we can't not be optimistic about this squad after what we saw in Week 8. That momentum (especially from Cam Ward) taken with Coach Saleh's lofty post-bye goals creates a mixture for excitement when Jacksonville comes to town.
Trade Ridley, fuel Ward, and open the door for a real statement after the week off. We'll see if the Titans' brass shares a similar sentiment in two days' time.

title: Last Looks: Where the Titans Stand 48 Hours Before the NFL Trade Deadline
full_text:
For the first time this season, the Tennessee Titans aren’t playing football this Sunday. On the bye today, all Titans fans have to do is sit back and wonder what’s next for this franchise. The trade deadline is in two days.
Instead of covering another one-score game throughout the day today, we’re taking a temperature check of sorts on Tennessee as the trade clock winds down to November 10.
As best we can tell, here’s where the Titans stand ahead of the deadline. We’ll start with one guy who is likely to have played his last game with Tennessee.
The cards have stacked against Calvin Ridley at this point, as far as trade news goes. After Adam Schefter reported yesterday that Ridley could be had for a sixth-round pick, Tom Pelissero followed that up with a report of his own. The latter went as far to say that he belives Ridley is likely to be traded.
The veteran WR has lost his place in this Titans’ offense, and doesn’t fit the picture of Tennessee’s ongoing rebuild any longer. Options like Elic Ayomanor and Chimere Dike have already begun to overshadow him.
Tennessee has more than one reason to move him, and suitors like the Kansas City Chiefs, among others, could certainly afford his cheap price tag to bulk up before the postseason.
It’s reasonable to think at this point that someone will make it work with the Titans. If anyone can be deemed a probable move, it’s Ridley.
To flip the script, RB Tony Pollard has worked his way into the “unlikely” category before the deadline, and that would be at best for any team trying to get him out of Nasvhille. Yesterday, the aforementioned Schefter outright said that the Titans "are not interested" in moving Pollard.
The Titans weren't interested in moving Jeffery Simmons either, but then again, no team is going to cough up two first-round picks for Pollard. This hill is much easier for Tennessee to stay standing on.
A team could potentially get desperate for RB help and send a convincing offer, especially if star back Jonathan Taylor ends up staying put in Indianapolis. But even in that case, you'd have to think the pick would be higher than the previously reported fourth-round rate for Pollard.
It's just hard to believe that a 29-year old back in the final year of his contract would go for more than that anywhere. Barring a truly unexpected shift, Titans fans can comfortably anticipate the rising RB to remain with Tennessee after November 10.
Beyond Ridley and Pollard, trade-candidate names have mostly fallen to the wayside for Tennessee. S Amani Hooker isn't available, as far as we know, and CB Alontae Taylor is more valuable than ever after his solid Week 8 showing and CB Marcus Harris' ankle injury.
It wouldn't be necessarily stunning if, say, LB Cody Barton were moved for a mid-to-late draft selection, but the Titans don't appear to be in any hurry to clear out on the defensive side of the ball.
Jacob Martin has been mentioned on the defensive line, but with Simmons gone, the Titans would be better off holding their sack leader for at least the rest of the year. The Simmons deal proved that nothing is impossible in the NFL, but at this point, don't expect much more trade noise from Tennessee.
Lane covers the Tennessee Titans, where he brings an evolving team's journey to fans on a daily basis. A longtime sports fanatic and recent baby blue jersey aficionado.

title: Commanders Daily: Washington Was Short on Receivers. Where Was Stefon Diggs?
full_text:
Heading into the Rams game on Sunday, the Washington Commanders were short on receivers: Terry McLaurin is out for the season, Treylon Burks is out, and Dyami Brown moved to injured reserve. Sounds like a day for Stefon Diggs to shine, right? The problem is Diggs' first catch, a four-yard burner, came with 7:28 left in the third quarter; he wouldn't gain another yard until a five-yarder with 4:41 left in the game. With 52 seconds remaining, they found him again for a 42-yard catch that moved Washington from its own 9 to the Rams' 49 and put the team in position to tie the game. When asked Monday why Diggs only had the one catch entering the final five minutes, Quinn responded by saying, "Yeah. I love his fire, man. Ben, I really do. And the competitive part. So he hit a couple targets earlier, and some that maybe he’s also first in the read to get there. Or for whatever reason, you know, you have to get off that. Or, you know, the read wasn’t there; the coverage took you somewhere else. So he’s definitely, like, in the front of our thinking. And so we need him, you know. And so that’s why he’s in the front of our thinking in those critical spots. So, you know, certainly one towards the end, you know, that gives us a chance to go after it. But, no, he’s always in the front of our thoughts. I love his fire. I love what he brings. And, like most excellent players, like as many opps as you can." Quinn is saying Diggs was the first read on some plays and that coverage pushed Daniels elsewhere on others. That is the politically correct response, but it still doesn't explain why Diggs had only four yards with five minutes left.
"You wish them nothing but the worst" 🤣 Stefon Diggs weighed in on how aware he is of the Commanders place in the NFC East. pic.twitter.com/WqWdICiBQT
After McLaurin’s injury, Quinn said he didn’t expect Diggs’ workload to increase much and pointed to rookie Antonio Williams as a player in line for more opportunities. The snap counts from the Rams game check out: Diggs played 38 of Washington's 62 offensive snaps against Los Angeles, while Williams played 52 and Van Jefferson had 36. Diggs had played 39 of 60 snaps against Philadelphia a week earlier, when Burks and Brown were both available. Even with those two out against Los Angeles, his snap share stayed about the same. Asked whether the two- and three-tight-end packages were why Diggs played less in the first half, Quinn said it wasn’t part of a deliberate design. Diggs missed the first game against New York that ended in a 27-27 tie, meaning Thursday will be his first game against the Giants in the burgundy and gold. The question is: Can Washington connect with Diggs earlier on the opportunities intended for him? His 42-yarder showed what one connection could change, but it arrived with less than a minute left against Los Angeles, a team without its top two cornerbacks .

title: Hughes’ View: The Commanders’ Center Gamble Left Jayden Daniels Exposed
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have hit that point in the season where, at 2-5-1, it's over unless they start winning, and the Giants and Cowboys have a massive fallout. Which could happen, but shouldn't be depended on under normal circumstances. For Washington, they have to ask themselves, how did they get here? Their latest issue on the offensive line stems from the center position: this past weekend, when their starter Lucas Patrick went down with a concussion, they turned to rookie Matt Gulbin. It's ironic because Adam Peters and Dan Quinn spent the offseason trying to convince everyone that Nick Allegretti was that guy and would be the center for 2026. Allegretti has played two snaps since his last start, which came at right guard against the Seattle Seahawks in Week 3. In other words, he's still the same journeyman offensive lineman who came here years ago looking for a chance to start, but better suited as a backup. They tried to sell the fanbase a pumpkin, hoping Cinderella logic would kick in and he'd turn into something more than a dried-up gourd that rots on a warm fall night.
To understand this mistake in motion, you first have to remember that the team's center in 2025, Tyler Biadasz, was abruptly released before free agency, not long before the team struck out on free agent Tyler Linderbaum , who signed with the Raiders. That led the team to Allegretti as the answer, even though he played only 78 NFL snaps at center before 2025 and then started the final two games that season. No reason has ever been given for Biadasz being cut, and Peters dodged rehashing any of it in all of his offseason pressers, but Peters' plan beyond Linderbaum was clearly flawed. After roster cuts, Peters said , "And that's where we went into this offseason feeling that Nick could be our starter, and still do feel that way." Drafting Gulbin in the sixth round may prove to be a great move in the future, but what about protecting your franchise quarterback now? The problem looked at least temporarily fixed when Lucas Patrick stepped into the role against Seattle . Washington had signed Patrick just 11 days before that start. In that game, right guard Sam Cosmi couldn't go, so it made sense to slide Allegretti over. The next week in London, Patrick stayed at center, and Gulbin slid over to right guard. That signaled Patrick had already taken over for the offseason starter, though Quinn initially called the change temporary before naming Patrick the starter the following Friday.
When asked about the situation Sunday after the game , Quinn said the staff has been working Allegretti more at guard now: "In that moment, I would have felt comfortable with Nick as well, but I thought, let’s give the guy who’s got the most reps." Quinn also confirmed Allegretti was healthy. It makes sense that the coach would turn to the player who has practiced the most in the role; the problem is he said this in the preseason: "Nick is one of our smartest players, so that's a position that you rely on." Relied on so much that when the team looks for a replacement weeks later in crunch time with the season on the line, they turn to the sixth-round prospect with very little experience. Gulbin gave up a 12-yard sack to Myles Garrett on third-and-5 at the Rams’ 38, leaving Washington facing fourth-and-17, but who could be mad at a rookie who should have been given more help on that play? The Commanders' protection plan failed when it mattered most Sunday; that's not to say there wasn't effort; it is to say the coaches didn't do their jobs.
Myles Garrett showed Rams fans what they traded for, dominating in his return from injury. 3 SACK, 1 FF vs Commanders. With Garrett back, could the 5-4 Rams make a serious run at winning the NFC? https://t.co/6sIEtDYadN pic.twitter.com/9E0DPtT6qM
Thursday night in New York will tell us whether anybody learned from this. Patrick is in concussion protocol, and Quinn has three days to decide who gets the next snap and what kind of help he’ll have. The Giants are leading the division. They won’t wait while Washington figures it out on the fly. If the rush gets home again because the staff leaves its center on an island, Daniels will be the one paying for decisions he didn’t make. Nine games left sounds hopeful until your quarterback spends the first of them running from the same problem you promised was solved.
