title: Commanders Report Card: Washington Went Short on Its Last Shot to Tie the Rams
full_text:
File the Washington Commanders' 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams away with the growing annals of painfully close defeats lining their 2-5-1 campaign, right alongside their season-opening outing against the Philadelphia Eagles, their Week 6 excursion against the San Francisco 49ers and that infamous link-up with the New York Giants, a technical tie that found a way to embarrass the fan base more than any 2026 matchup before or since.
The Rams looked exactly as advertised: talented, but never quite in sync. They entered the fourth quarter tied with their Landover hosts thanks to a slew of Commanders-esque holding penalties and miscues, yet still found a way to prevail following more late-game disappointments out of Washington. On which position groups gave it their all, and where criticism will continue to pile:
We expect a lot from Jayden Daniels , someone who's proven talented and clutch enough to drag his team into contention. And while he had highlights, this game still included a few nagging patterns that will continue to make wins tougher to pull off against anyone resembling a contender.
He made his 274 passing yards on a 101.4 passer rating against a Los Angeles defense that needed time to start looking the part, though a few lean quarters in the middle of the game did little to add to the Commanders' early success. He showed up in crunch time with his impressive accuracy and mobile escapability, as usual, reminding fans just how much they'd missed that downfield aggression between the seemingly endless slew of three-and-out punts.
Jayden Daniels & Stefon Diggs connect to move the Commanders close to midfield with 30 seconds to go LARvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SYNnMl9V9Z
That inconsistency has held him back from having his first truly great game of the season, even if he's been above average whenever he's taken the field this fall. The occasional goofs on his part certainly don't help, with one fumble, his first turnover of the season, setting up a Rams field goal before halftime. And on the snap before that disastrous attempted buzzer-beating touchdown, Daniels missed Stefon Diggs downfield after getting lucky on a few dropped potential interceptions.
While Quinn backed the short throw against pressure on the final snap, this streak of gaffes will only continue adding fuel to the fires of those questioning Daniels' situational awareness.
Jacory "Bill" Croskey-Merritt is still on the shelf, leaving a hodgepodge of reserves in Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler to ease Daniels' burden on the ground. They ended up being arguably more effective as dump-off options on a few short passes than they were at navigating dogpiles, finding ways to evade deadly Rams tacklers while failing to back up the coaching staff's insistence on deploying them to start every series.
44 total rushing yards on a combined carry count of 15 still isn't nearly enough to match up against any serious defense, though, and they've been lucky to get nearly as much as they have out of the aging Ekeler a little over a year after he tore his Achilles tendon. Very little between the remaining talent and the blockers creating the holes being dashed through has impressed this season, leaving this piece of the offense to predictably struggle against a team with the Rams' pedigree and depth.
Van Jefferson's doing a lot of heavy lifting in this category, a situation no one could have fathomed he'd slide before the season started. He was one of the final casualties of the preseason cut wave, falling short of the seven-man receiver room that includes the recently injured Terry McLaurin, Jaylin Lane, Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown, as well as Luke McCaffrey, who's since been relegated to the group's full-time return man.
Left without much of anyone to turn to outside of Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams, who each did enough given their limited targets, the coaching staff somehow struck gold in their last-minute turn to Jefferson. Against a Rams team with whom he'd once won Super Bowl LVI, he stacked a Washington-high 58 yards on five catches, including his first touchdown in the burgundy and gold.
first one of the season for Van Jefferson 🙌 📺 #LARvsWAS FOX pic.twitter.com/7SbDhDOCZy
Chig Okonkwo, similarly, showed up big in this one, coming just one yard short of Jefferson's finish with a handful of his typically athletic moves after the catch. Even if the pass-catching resource pool was depleted this week, the Commanders would be better off leaning more on the downfield attack- at least, if he knows that he's getting enough protection to enjoy the luxury of waiting for his reads to form.
I find it harder than usual to fault Daniels' protective line for this one, as the remaining offensive linemen did stand up for themselves somewhat in the face of a few legendary pass-rushers. Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald repeatedly squared up on the same side of Los Angeles' defense, forcing Washington's hand in choosing which former Defensive Player of the Year winner to double.
Unfortunately for Daniels, and predictably to everyone else, Brandon Coleman was no match for Garrett in his three-sack return to action. Few can hold up to that combination of size and speed, but the fresh round of false starts certainly does wonders for his image in the eyes of the frustrated fan base still pining for usual starter Laremy Tunsil.
Throw in yet another center, rookie Matt Gulbin, to fill in for the hurt Lucas Patrick, and we're left with more questions beyond Garrett's most lopsided matchup partner. How could a front office that was so in on Nick Allegretti as their center through the offseason be this comfortable skipping over him so regularly in parsing through the depth chart? Another dilemma worth investigating amidst the season's nosedive.
Washington Commanders killer Matthew Stafford didn't look like he was having a great time on Northwest Stadium's grass. He threw a pick right at Nick Cross, got bumped into a sack, and required 43 attempts to reach 228 yards; that stat line included a litany of missed connections with his streaking receivers.
K'Lavon Chaisson with a textbook punch out LARvsWAS on FOX/FOX One Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/tu0FRD6Xux
Washington's defensive linemen and backers deserve some credit for at least making it tough on them, and for holding Kyren Williams to 45 yards on 15 carries while more efficient understudy Blake Corum went for 58 on 11, though they did lack some of that same blitzing bite without the Rams' willingness to regularly throw to screens off to the sides of the hashes.
They held their opponents to 3/14 on third downs to give their offense plenty of chances to respond. Still, reigning MVP Stafford is as unafraid to heave down the gut of opposing defenses, a problem that ended up falling on the secondary.
It's hard to pay the back-line defenders too much grace when they didn't even have Davante Adams to occupy their attention, yet they still found a way to allow 150 yards to Puka Nacua. As K'Lavon Chaisson put it after the game, the Rams were “running the same play all day, feeding the same person the ball all day.”
The Commanders could not stop Puka Nacua today. 14 catches for 150 yards and a TD. K'Lavon Chaisson said, "as a defense, you just gotta drop your nuts and figure out how you're going to stop that and not let it happen anymore." pic.twitter.com/vRH5DgbOtz
Ultimately, that admittedly successful playstyle reflects on everyone participating in the productive defense, and no individual defensive back could do much to disrupt Nacua's mission. The team didn't start doubling him on his downhill routes until deep into the outing, too talented to be treated like your average wideout with room to run after his completions.
Cross did his part with a fumble recovery and a pick, and Trey Amos did his part by playing generally good, tight coverage, albeit not as tightly as he played in last week's win over the Eagles. There are pieces…

title: Everything Dan Quinn Said After Commanders’ Loss to Rams
full_text:
The Washington Commanders had two plays from the Rams’ 31 to get into the end zone Sunday. Jayden Daniels threw an incomplete pass to Stefon Diggs with eight seconds left, then went underneath to Chig Okonkwo with three seconds to play. Los Angeles recovered a fumble to seal a 20-13 win . Dan Quinn said Washington checked down to the short throw when the Rams showed pressure. He wanted better execution on the play. Washington fell to 2-5-1 and has a Thursday night rematch against the division-leading New York Giants in Week 10.
Opening statement “All right, let’s get rolling. Frustrating game, and once again, we have not nailed our complementary football, and I’ll keep saying it until we do. We’re halfway through the season, and that all has to click. After stops, don’t think we capitalized. We had two takeaways. I think we only got three points out of it. We had some opportunities for fourth-down stops defensively, to get those stops, to get it flipped the other way. So, all that said, it’s a short week against our division leader on the road, and we got to go and we have to play all three phases together. Seen too much of it where it’s part of it, not the whole thing. And so that’s what we’re going to continue to just practice, and that has to get right. It just has to. Too far along to not have it all working together. All right, let’s get rolling.” The offense got off to a pretty good start but seemed to fall flat. What was missing? “Yeah, I did like the way that we started, too, Nikki. I felt that way. To see us have some runs, have action to go, and I didn’t feel like we were able to sustain that. To get ahead and then here’s a chance even to get a takeaway and go further. But my biggest examples, even the complementary, we had a chance to be on our two-minute to go. We got a takeaway. I think it was maybe a fumble recovery, and then we turned it over again. They get a field goal. Looking back to it, I’ll give them credit, too. I want to watch the tape from a front standpoint, but I liked how we started. But just to not see that sustained, Nikki, that’s the thing that’s especially frustrating.” What went into your decision to challenge the third-quarter play involving Amik Robertson where the ruling was upheld? "After review they thought maybe it was bobbled on the first step. So then that didn't make it into the second step meaning that became the first." "But I think on those ones sometimes like you have to take a shot too. You know when it's a one that you think is reasonable to go when it's clear and obvious many times that gets replay assisted but in that moment I felt like this was one if it's close roll the dice." On the final play, what went into the decision to go with the lateral play instead of taking a shot directly at the end zone? “Yeah. So, there’s two plays that you come in. And so, on the first one, you’re taking a shot to the end zone, just like you described. And sometimes to check for that against a team that does what we call a zero blitz or a max blitz, you want to, ‘OK, here’s the other play where you can’t block them all up.’” “So we got to the second play of what would have been, like, everybody blitzing, check it down and move forward from there. So with eight seconds left, you want two chances at something. And so to not have those, didn’t love our execution at our end.” Lucas Patrick and Amik Robertson went down during the game. Do you have an update on either of them? “The only one I do have is that, with Lucas not coming back, he’s in the concussion protocol. But I’ll give you some updates tomorrow whenever we talk next regarding anyone else. That’s the only one that the medical team hit me on prior to tonight.” A couple of players said they knew what the Rams were going to do on offense, with the inside runs and getting the ball to Puka Nacua. Why was that so hard to stop? “Yeah, yeah, for sure. And I give him credit, too. So the inside style of runs, I guess that’s what they’ve been demonstrating. And I knew that was going to be one of the strengths of their team. I thought both the backs had showed good production doing that. With Nacua, I knew there had also been some on the screen side of things. So it’s not all dropbacks to go. And I think that’s part of what makes him unique is his catch-and-run ability, where it’s not just downfield throws. So on those, you have to be able to roll up and tackle well, John, too. He may get X number of catches for not too far down the field, but knowing that, ‘Hey, man, you got to go get your tackle.’ So having too many yards, that was big for me.”
There are still nine games left. Do you feel like you’re running out of time to turn this around? “Yeah, I think it speaks to the importance of a division leader right away. And so it’s a difficult locker room. We got to turn the page quickly to get to that because we talked earlier, ‘OK, this is where we are,’ but we also know, ‘Man, we have to play at our best.’” How difficult was that spot for Matt Gulbin to come into? How well has he practiced to earn the backup spot, and is Nick Allegretti still an option at center? “In that moment, I would have felt comfortable with Nick as well, but I thought, let’s give the guy who’s got the most reps. That was the decision behind it. It’s difficult, but … this is part of the gig.” Brandon Coleman had a couple of penalties again. In the middle of a game, how do you decide when to put somebody else in if a player is struggling? “Yes. And I want to go back to look. We’ve put a lot of work … what could change to get some of these false starts off. So to have still two remain. I think Sam’s might have been a holding, right, on that one that was prior to the turnover. We’ve made adjustments on how many cadences, what types and that. So I just want to see if it’s a product of too much anticipation against a good rusher. And that’s different to me than a lack of focus. That makes sense, Dave. I’ll give you a better answer once I have a chance to look at him.” Just to be clear on Allegretti, he’s healthy? “Yes. Yeah, yeah. We’ve just been working him more at guard and Matt at center. And, you know, if we have to change, we’ll see what next week looks like as well.” Going back to the last two plays, you mentioned you didn’t like the execution. Was the final play called that way, or was it a check Jayden Daniels made based on what he saw? “Yeah, it has to be one that you get to a second play, and it’s the right adjustment to make it and going. So how long do you wait? You get the full protection and try to throw a Hail Mary, because it’s hard to, on a Hail Mary, get everybody scrambling and buy time when they’re bringing everyone. So that’s the juxtapose of, like, get to a max protection, buy time, or that’s another alternative play. The one before it was really the one I wanted to see more execution when there was maybe eight seconds at that point. There’s just two plays remaining in the game, and you want to give yourself a chance.” Did that call have to do with the Rams keeping three defenders across the goal line on the previous play and expecting to see that again? “I think just more tape history, too, of what could be and what they’ve done.” You were shorthanded at receiver , and it looked like Stefon Diggs played less in the first half while you used a lot of 12 and 13 personnel. Was that part of the plan? “No. No, it wasn’t any further design than another.” Van Jefferson went from the practice squad and having no catches coming in to being one of your leading receivers, especially in the first half. How much of that did you anticipate? “Yeah, I wouldn’t say it was anticipated, Ben, but I would say this is somebody that is a respected player around here. And I can remember after camp having a hard conversation and him coming back on a practice squad when we had a very healthy wide receiver room, knowing it would take a leap of faith to still come, knowing that there were six players already…

title: Commanders Instant Takeaways: Washington’s Offense Let the Rams Off the Hook | Game Pulse
full_text:
The Washington Commanders led 10-6 at halftime Sunday and scored just three points the rest of the way, losing 20-13 to the Los Angeles Rams at Northwest Stadium. The loss dropped Washington to 2-5-1. Both Washington takeaways gave the offense the ball in Rams territory. All the Commanders got out of them was a Drew Stevens field goal. They still got the ball twice in the final six minutes with a chance to tie. The Giants beat Philadelphia 19-11 to move three games ahead of Washington in the NFC East. The Commanders get their rematch Thursday night at MetLife Stadium. Here are my immediate reactions in this week’s Game Pulse. *Game Pulse collects my instant takeaways after each quarter and at the final whistle.
- Washington needed a better answer for Myles Garrett. He finished with three sacks, and the one that hurt most came when he beat rookie center Matt Gulbin and turned third-and-5 at the Rams’ 38 into fourth-and-17. With Lucas Patrick out and a chance to tie the game, I wanted more help for Gulbin in that spot. - I wanted to see Washington double Puka Nacua more. He caught 14 of 19 targets for 150 yards and the go-ahead touchdown. Stafford kept going back to him. At some point, you have to make somebody else beat you.
The Commanders could not stop Puka Nacua today. 14 catches for 150 yards and a TD. K'Lavon Chaisson said, "as a defense, you just gotta drop your nuts and figure out how you're going to stop that and not let it happen anymore." pic.twitter.com/vRH5DgbOtz
- I liked how Washington played the run late. Sonny Styles and Shy Tuttle both made stops behind the line that helped force punts with the Rams trying to run the clock. Styles finished with 13 tackles and Frankie Luvu had 15. That defense gave the offense enough chances to tie it. - Van Jefferson gave Jayden Daniels a reliable option over the middle. He finished with five catches for 58 yards and Washington’s only touchdown, and both of his fourth-quarter catches went for first downs. He also had room on fourth-and-17. I thought Daniels left that one a little short, and Emmanuel Forbes got a hand on it. - I wanted the ball in the end zone on the last snap. Stefon Diggs’ 42-yard catch gave Washington a real chance after it took over at its own 9 with 52 seconds left and no timeouts. With three seconds left from the Rams’ 31, the ball went to Chig Okonkwo short of the goal line, and the Rams recovered a half-hearted attempt at a lateral that ended in a fumble.
End of game sequence was not ideal. WSH got to play he 32 and had two plays left. Neither throw was into end zone. The last play was designed to be short it looks like. Rams brought 5, one on a delay. But looks like routes weren’t vertical. Odd. pic.twitter.com/NLcy5kXil6
- Nick Cross has been Washington’s best defensive back today. He’s had a hand in both takeaways, and he made Stafford pay for trying to force one to Puka Nacua. I liked his work against Tyler Higbee, too. That was a third-down stop Washington had to challenge to get. - Washington went the whole quarter without a first down, even with the ball at the Rams’ 27 after the pick. Brandon Coleman’s false start helped put the offense in third-and-16. Drew Stevens did his job from 41 yards, but I wanted seven with that field position. - Holding the Rams without a conversion on their first nine third downs was good work. What bothered me was how easily they stayed out of third down coming out of halftime. Los Angeles went 69 yards for a touchdown without facing one.
- I’d keep finding ways to get Rachaad White the ball. He turned a short throw into 45 yards to set up Van Jefferson’s touchdown, and he showed what he could do on the ground when John Bates opened a hole on that 14-yard run. With McLaurin out, White can take some of the work off Daniels. - Frankie Luvu has been Washington’s best defender so far. He got to Matthew Stafford for a nine-yard sack, and I liked seeing Jer’Zhan Newton get into the backfield on a run Luvu finished for a loss. That’s the push I wanted to see from Newton in his first game back. - Washington wasted a chance to go up two scores. K’Lavon Chaisson and Nick Cross gave the offense the ball at the Rams’ 40. Sam Cosmi’s hold wiped out a good run, and Myles Garrett forced Daniels’ first turnover of the season . A short field for Washington turned into three points for the Rams.
- That 15-yard throw from Jayden Daniels to Chig Okonkwo was textbook. With McLaurin out, I’d keep giving Daniels that option over the middle. - Both tackles gave me reason to worry. Brandon Coleman got beat on a run that lost four yards, and Josh Conerly Jr. wound up on the ground in pass protection. Daniels got the ball out, but he’s going to need more help against this front. - I liked how Frankie Luvu set the edge against the run. Holding the Rams to a field goal was a good result, but Washington can’t let Stafford stay on the field for 14 plays at a time.
- Myles Garrett is back alongside Aaron Donald, and Byron Young gives Los Angeles another way to get after Jayden Daniels. I’ll be watching how Washington handles first and second down. If the Commanders keep putting themselves in third-and-long, the Rams get to rush on their terms. - Trent McDuffie and Jaylen Watson are out, which is a break for Washington’s thin receiving group. I want to see Antonio Williams get work early again. If the Rams take away Williams and Stefon Diggs, where does Daniels go with the ball? Chig Okonkwo is one place to look. - Jer’Zhan Newton is back. How much he plays is the first thing I’ll be watching. If Washington can get a push inside with four rushers, Matthew Stafford has less room to step up when Washington’s edge rushers get around the tackles.
The Washington Commanders came into Sunday’s game against the Los Angeles Rams looking to build on their 27-10 win over Philadelphia . The Rams were missing both starting cornerbacks, but with Myles Garrett back, Washington had to give Jayden Daniels enough time to make those absences matter.

title: Commanders’ Depleted Receiving Corps Catches a Break Against Rams
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have only two available wide receivers who have caught a pass for them this season: Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams. Neither will have to face Trent McDuffie on Sunday. The Rams cornerback is inactive with a back injury, leaving Los Angeles down two starters at the position after Jaylen Watson went on injured reserve Saturday. Jer’Zhan Newton is active for his season debut. The defensive tackle missed Washington’s first seven games with a pectoral injury, practiced fully all week, and was activated from injured reserve Saturday . Here are the Week 9 inactive lists for both teams:
WR Treylon Burks QB Athan Kaliakmanis (emergency third quarterback) CB Fabian Moreau CB Isaac Yiadom G Tanoa Togiai
Treylon Burks was ruled out Friday with a foot injury. Washington placed Dyami Brown on injured reserve Saturday with a calf injury and elevated Jaden Bradley from the practice squad. Bradley is active, giving the Commanders depth at receiver, now that Terry McLaurin is also on injured reserve.
CB Trent McDuffie QB Ty Simpson LS Joe Cardona OLB Darryl Peterson III OL Bill Murray OL Keagan Trost OLB Desjuan Johnson
Los Angeles will have Myles Garrett available for the first time since Week 1. Safety Kam Curl and tight end Colby Parkinson are also active after being listed as questionable Friday. Tight end Terrance Ferguson remains on injured reserve.

title: Commanders vs. Rams Weather Forecast: Wind Could Matter Early
full_text:
Sunday looks like a good afternoon to be at Northwest Stadium. The Washington Commanders host the Los Angeles Rams with sunshine in the forecast and temperatures expected to stay in the low 60s during the game. The wind is worth keeping an eye on early, particularly when either team has a shot at a deep throw or a long field goal. Washington is 2-4-1 coming off its win over Philadelphia. The Rams are 4-4, and kickoff is scheduled for 1 p.m. ET Sunday, Nov. 8, in Landover, Maryland.
The National Weather Service’s hourly forecast for Landover has it at 61 degrees for kickoff, with a west wind around 11 mph and gusts up to 21 mph. Rain chances are listed at 0% through the game window, and sustained winds are expected to ease as the afternoon goes on. Forecast updated Saturday, Nov. 7, at 2:31 p.m. ET. All times are Eastern.
9 a.m. — parking lots open
11 a.m. — stadium gates open
Washington is already working around injuries at receiver , and giving Jayden Daniels time against the Rams’ pass rush is the first concern when it wants to throw deep. If the Commanders get a clean pocket, the gusts are worth accounting for. A ball that stays in the air longer gives the wind more time to move it. Drew Stevens has already hit from 57 yards at Northwest Stadium, but the wind could change what feels like a reasonable attempt early Sunday. A kick into the wind can lose carry, while the same breeze could help from the other end. Warmups should give Stevens and Dan Quinn a better idea of his range in each direction.
The Commanders’ gameday guide lists the RedZone lot opening at 8 a.m., general parking at 9 a.m., Legends Plaza at 10 a.m. and stadium gates at 11 a.m. It could be around 46 degrees when the RedZone lot opens and 52 when the other lots open, with a breeze through the morning. Bring a light jacket if you’re tailgating. By the time you’re in your seat for kickoff, it should be in the low 60s. title: How to Watch Commanders vs. Rams: TV Channel, Start Time, Streaming, and Radio
full_text:
The Washington Commanders return to Northwest Stadium Sunday to face the Los Angeles Rams after scoring 27 unanswered points in their 27-10 win over the Philadelphia Eagles last week. Washington enters the matchup at 2-4-1, while the Rams come to town at 4-4. The Commanders will be without two more receivers Sunday after Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown were ruled out Friday. Terry McLaurin is already out for the season, leaving Stefon Diggs and Antonio Williams as the only available receivers on Washington's roster who have caught a pass for the team this season. Los Angeles has injury concerns of its own, although the Rams activated Myles Garrett from injured reserve Saturday. Here is everything you need to know to watch, stream, and listen to the Commanders' Week 9 matchup against the Rams.
Date: Sunday, Nov. 8 Kickoff: 1:00 p.m. ET Location: Northwest Stadium, Landover, Maryland TV: FOX Weather Report : Wind could be an issue .
Outfit repeaters pic.twitter.com/kMkrv4KyHg
FOX will carry Sunday's game in select television markets. Fans should check their local FOX listings to confirm availability. Play-by-play: Chris Myers Analyst: Mark Schlereth Sideline: Jen Hale In the Washington, D.C., market, the game will air on FOX 5 (WTTG). Los Angeles viewers can watch on FOX 11 (KTTV). Fans outside those markets should check their local FOX listings for coverage.

title: 10 Commanders Quotes Show Receiver Injuries Aren't Washington's Only Problem
full_text:
The Washington Commanders have a win to build on after beating the Philadelphia Eagles, but they have a new set of problems to deal with before the Los Angeles Rams visit Sunday. Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown have been ruled out , leaving Jayden Daniels with a depleted receiving corps. The Rams have Aaron Donald, Myles Garrett is expected back, and Matthew Stafford presents a different challenge for a Washington defense coming off its best pass-rushing performance of the season. From Stefon Diggs trying to explain the offense's slow starts to Dan Quinn discussing the limitations of Washington's receiver depth, this week's press conferences provided plenty to consider. Here are 10 quotes that help define where the Commanders stand entering Week 9.
Question: What does Daniels admire about Matthew Stafford's game, and has he learned anything from their relationship over the years? “Yeah, I mean, me and him have a good relationship over the years. You know, we trained at the same spot in Southern California. But just the way he's able to spin a football and, you know, have so much control over a football. You know, one day I hope to get there. But it's just so much respect and admiration for his game and, you know, how he plays the position.”
Question: What makes Stafford difficult to defend, particularly with his experience reading coverages and manipulating defenders? “Yeah, I mean, obviously he's been playing for a long time. So he's seen a lot of different looks, a lot of different defenses. So disguise is going to be at a premium. Got to be able to disguise really well. Make the look a little different pre-snap than what he sees post-snap. You know, he does a really good job with ball placement. Also does a really good job of manipulating using his eyes and his body language. Think he's going to throw it one way, ends up throwing it the other way. So, just being really disciplined in your zone. Like, sometimes his eyes are going to lie to you. You feel like he's looking one way, he sees that route that you're working away from. So, just being disciplined in whatever your assignment is.”
Question: How does Puka Nacua's physicality and ability to work across the formation affect Washington's linebackers? “Yeah, man, you know, Puka, he's like another running back. You know what I mean? He gets a lot of contact, you know, get the balls out, screens and a lot of perimeter stuff. Take the top off, in-breaking. So, like, he's that piece that glues everything together. So, you know, it's tough. But, man, like, respect to him. You know what I mean? But in our aspect, we've just got to keep him in the phone booth , and we'll be all right.”
Question: Against a quarterback as experienced as Stafford, does Washington need to increase its pressure or be more selective about when it blitzes? “Well, I'm sure a lot of defenses have tried that to speed him up, so to speak, but he's already sped up. I mean, the one thing about Stafford is his ability, he has the no-look passes. He understands, he has a clock in his head, and so everything has to be calculated when you wanna send pressure, when you don't, when you wanna have the front, when you wanna have the illusion of it. And so it becomes more of a chess match in that light, more so just having blitzes just for the sake of blitzing.”
Question: With the receiver injuries creating a larger potential role for Van Jefferson, how important was his decision to return to Washington despite having other opportunities? “I told him, I think it was before he came up, I said, I really appreciate him putting his trust in us to come back here. We knew it was a deep group during training camp. And so he wasn't here the first time on our practice squad. And I knew there would be a little bit of a leap of faith knowing he was going to come back on the practice squad. It was still a deep group that we had. And sure enough, here it is where he was going to commit to it, even though this may not happen where he had chances to go play. But I liked his approach. I liked his readiness. And so when called upon, I'd expect he'd play well based on how much he stayed into it. And so I think just for me, the gratitude for him staying to it.”
Question: Washington has started slowly in consecutive games. How does the offense correct those problems when the team believes it has practiced well during the week? “Sh*t, I don't know. I mean, I think just in practice, I wouldn't even say that because we stack some good days in practice, and you go in the game. I don't know. You might have a little bit of this/that here and there, but it seems like we just kind of got to hone in on the details. And, you know, when I say execute better, it's all of us. So, I don't know. There's no magic wand to do it. We just got to, you know, go in the game with the right mindset and everybody play as one.”
Question: How close is Daniels to mastering Washington's new offensive system, particularly the mental responsibilities that come with playing quarterback? “We talk about this a lot. We talk about quarterbacks in their prime and probably not hitting it mentally until you're into your 30s. So he is learning a new language, truthfully. And there was a ton of growth in May and June, and there's a ton of growth every week now. So I wouldn't say mastery is there, but it's not there for anybody, any quarterback in this league who's getting to play in new systems. And so that's the fun part for us is kind of chasing the comfort of understanding the system. ”
Question: Against a premium defensive lineman like Donald, what problems arise when an offense commits additional blockers to double-team him? “Yeah, I mean, the thing they've got, they've got a lot of really good defensive linemen . Zero's rushing the quarterback at an elite rate, 95's back on the field. He's a premium player. There's a lot of really good rushers. And give credit to their coaching staff, too. They don't just allow you to always double-team Aaron Donald. So we're gonna have to be really intentional with our protection plan to handle what they do up front. And it's a great challenge, man. They do a really good job.”
Question: After Daniels gathered his teammates on the sideline against Philadelphia, how does he maintain that sense of urgency and accountability throughout the week? “Yeah, I think it's just that same urgency throughout the week. And I'm not saying that we don't have that. But, you know, we've got to stop shooting ourselves in the foot. And it starts with practice, starts with the accountability from, you know, myself to the other 10 guys in the huddle. And just let them know, like, nobody's bigger than the standard that we have set. And if you mess up or, you know, stuff like that, you know, there's going to be consequences for it.”
Question: With only two available receivers who have caught passes for Washington this season, how does the team compensate for the lack of game experience among the other options? “Yeah, they've caught a lot in practice. I would say that. I don't think there's a way to compensate in that for the game, Nikki, but going into it to have the trust to get into it, it is part of what we do when we think of our 70-man roster. It's not these guys here, these guys here. So being part of that, and these are those times where it does benefit to say like everybody gets reps, everybody's playing. So there's not a natural tendency to work back to not put in the work for that game plan just because you just don't know when a moment comes up when you need to do it.”
Washington recovered from a 10-point deficit against Philadelphia, but the problems that contributed to that slow start haven't disappeared. Injuries have also forced the coaching staff to reconsider how it distributes opportunities on offense. The Rams bring a different set of challenges on both sides of the ball. What Washington has emphasized throughout the week—communication, execution, and preparation…
